title: UX Research Debriefs Reframed
intro: Teams merge two kinds of research debrief to save time and get the worst of both. Calabro separates them: a **synthesis session** to make sense of data, then a **strategic session** to decide.

learn.title: Type 1: Synthesis session
learn.text:
Happens right after data collection, while observations are fresh.

**Who:** researchers, one or two designers, a PM comfortable with open-ended discussion.
**How:** evidence visible (quotes, screenshots, clips); look for patterns.
**Close with:** what we know, what we think, what we need to verify.

Keep it deliberately open-ended.

try.q: How should a synthesis session end?
options: What we know, think, and need to verify
A ranked list of features to build next
A sign-off from the product leadership
A final slide deck for all stakeholders
try.explain: It produces themes and open questions, not next steps.

learn.title: Type 2: Strategic session
learn.text:
Once findings are synthesised, the purpose shifts to alignment and action. A clear sequence:

**Finding** → **Implication** → **Decision needed**

Example: appraisers worked in three unofficial stages → re-architect navigation around those stages → validate with a low-fidelity prototype before committing engineering time.

try.q: In a strategic debrief, what follows the finding?
options: Its implication, then the decision needed
The full method, sample and recruiting details
A vote on whether the finding is true
All remaining raw quotes and clips

learn.title: Why mixing them fails
learn.text:
When synthesis and strategy are blended, three things happen:

• Leaders expecting answers **lose patience with ambiguity**
• Researchers get **derailed into solutions** before the evidence is solid
• **Action items rest on half-baked insights**

try.q: A VP joins your first look at raw interview notes and starts proposing fixes. Which problem is this?
options: Researchers derailed before evidence is solid
The VP has not read the research plan
The session has too few participants
The notes were not transcribed and tagged in time
try.explain: Solutions arrive before the analysis is done.

test.q: Who belongs in a synthesis session?
options: A small group at ease with open questions
Every stakeholder affected by the project
Only executives who own the budget
Customers who took part in the study
test.explain: Researchers, one or two designers, an open-minded PM.

test.q: What is the purpose of a strategic debrief?
options: Alignment and action
Finding patterns in raw data
Training new team members
Recruiting for the next study
test.explain: It turns settled findings into decisions.

test.q: Why do teams merge the two debriefs?
options: To save time
Because research guidelines require it
Because findings are usually simple
To keep designers out of the room
test.explain: It seems efficient on paper and costs more in practice.

test.q: What else does a good strategic session surface?
options: Trade-offs, such as tech debt blocking a fix
Every usability issue ever recorded
The researcher's personal design preferences, in full
A new list of research questions only
test.explain: Sometimes a finding can't be addressed yet; that is discussed openly.

test.q: Which is NOT a result of mixing synthesis and strategy?
options: Findings become statistically significant
Leaders lose patience with ambiguity
Researchers get pulled into solutions early
Action items rest on half-baked insights
test.explain: The other three are the failures Calabro lists.
